---
title: "Theory"
subtitle: "Model assumptions and the connection to measured intensity"
---

These concepts help you decide what a model represents and how to compare its
prediction with an experiment. The [Tutorials](tutorials/index.qmd) apply them
to concrete models; the [Reference Wiki](https://github.com/Tobionecenobi/pySEB/wiki)
provides detailed definitions and API documentation.

## Model assumptions

A model specifies both scattering material and the statistics of its geometry.
A reference identifies an attachment location; a distributed reference
specifies a statistical selection over locations. The subunits and their
connections determine the distances that enter the scattering calculation.

A 3D view shows one realization. Its displayed polymer conformation and
sampled attachment positions are examples of the ensemble used by the model.
An overlap-reduced display layout changes the illustration rather than adding
excluded-volume interactions to the scattering calculation.

Start with [What is a reference point?](tutorials/reference-points.qmd) to
separate scattering material from attachment locations. For the compositional
formalism, graph constraints, and reference statistics, read the Wiki's
[Core Concepts](https://github.com/Tobionecenobi/pySEB/wiki/Core-Concepts) and
[Theory Overview](https://github.com/Tobionecenobi/pySEB/wiki/Theory-Overview).

## From form factor to measured intensity

The normalized form factor describes the shape of a scattering curve.
The unnormalized single-particle scattering also retains the excess scattering
lengths. For total excess scattering length $\beta\ne0$,

$$
I_{\mathrm{single}}(q)=\beta^2 F(q).
$$

For identical, dilute, independently positioned particles with number density
$n$, the corresponding intensity per volume is

$$
I(q)=n\,I_{\mathrm{single}}(q)+B(q),
$$

in consistent units, where $B(q)$ is the background. For a homogeneous region,
$\beta=(\rho-\rho_{\mathrm{solvent}})V$, using its scattering-length density
contrast and volume. Absolute-intensity comparison requires consistent
scattering-length, volume, and reciprocal-length units.

Particle-size distributions, interparticle correlations, and measurement
resolution require their own treatment. A scale factor alone does not supply
those effects. The [sasmodels integration](sasmodels.qmd) describes its explicit
distribution, interaction, and resolution options.

For API definitions, see [Scattering Quantities](https://github.com/Tobionecenobi/pySEB/wiki/Scattering-Quantities).
For a worked conversion using contrast, volume fraction, unit conversion, and
background, follow [Fit real contrast-variation SANS data](tutorials/fit-real-sans-data.qmd#convert-contrast-into-excess-scattering-length).
[SasView’s sphere-model definition](https://www.sasview.org/docs/user/models/sphere.html)
also shows this volume-fraction, contrast, and background convention explicitly.
